title: F.TEST is twice the smaller tail of the larger-first ratio; swapping the arrays moves the last bit on ties
statement: F.TEST returns 2 * min(P(F > f), P(F <= f)) for the variance ratio f taken larger variance first, not min(2 * P(F > f), 1). With unequal degrees of freedom the right tail of the larger-first ratio can pass 1/2 even at f = 1 (equal variances, sizes 5 and 3), where the clamped form returns 1; Excel build 20228 returns 0.888888888888889 there. DNA Calc computes both tails from the one incomplete-beta call that F.DIST.RT's staging uses, taking its own complement output rather than 1 - p: that held 13 gross full-bank rows (up to 1.8e15 units off before) and took F.TEST from 21 to 26 matched of 78 with the worst miss from 1,767,616,520,413,419 units to 11, gaining 5 and losing none; the other 8 former gross rows are now 1 to 8 units off. Not ordering the ratio larger-first (var1/var2 as given) lost 8 matched rows. Equal variances give the same value with either argument order up to the last bit: the recorded answers for the two orders of the same arrays are 0x3fec71c71c71c71e and 0x3fec71c71c71c71c. A rule that orients exact ties with var1 > var2 was measured and not taken (+4 and -3 of 78 rows, against an estimate of +6 and -3).
basis: Two recorded Excel build 20228 rows (the same arrays in both argument orders) are cited; DNA Calc returns the second of them, and four further recorded rows are held in DNA Calc's unit test. Row counts are quoted from the commit messages (full bank, row-by-row trace).
inferred: That Excel orients the ratio larger-first and takes both tails from one incomplete-beta call is inferred from the match counts; 'ties' here means equal sample variances, and Excel's rule for choosing the orientation on them is not identified.
